chunks.title: Collision or accident damage
chunks.text:
After any collision: if anyone may be hurt, call 108 (ambulance) or 112 first, before anything else.

Switch off the engine, switch on hazard lights, and move uninjured people away from traffic. Do not move an injured person unless there is an immediate danger such as fire.

Do not drive a vehicle after a collision until it has been checked, even if it looks fine. Leaking fluids, damaged steering or a damaged wheel may not be visible.

chunks.title: Collision or accident damage
chunks.text: Take photos of the scene and the vehicles only when it is safe to do so. The vehicle will usually need towing.

chunks.title: Alternator or charging system failure
chunks.text:
Signs: battery warning light comes on while driving, lights dim or flicker, electrics fail one by one, then the engine stops. Words drivers use: battery light, charging nahi ho raha, dynamo, died while driving.

Once the alternator fails the vehicle is running only on the battery, which will run out. Pull over safely while you still have lights and hazards.

chunks.title: Alternator or charging system failure
chunks.text:
This usually needs a replacement alternator or belt, which is often not a quick roadside job. A mechanic may be able to charge or swap the battery to get you to a workshop.

Keep one phone switched off as a reserve so you can still call for help later.

chunks.title: Dead battery or no crank
chunks.text:
Signs: the engine does not turn over, you hear only clicking, dashboard lights are dim or dead. Words drivers use: battery dead, self nahi le raha, not starting, gaadi start nahi ho rahi, click click.

Switch off AC, music and headlights so any remaining charge is kept for the restart. Keep hazard lights on for visibility; they draw little power.

chunks.title: Dead battery or no crank
chunks.text:
A mechanic can usually jump-start the vehicle or fit a new battery at the roadside. If the battery dies again soon after a jump start, the charging system (alternator) may be the real cause.

Do not attempt a jump start yourself unless you know the correct connection order. See the jump-start safety guide.

chunks.title: Brake failure or brake fluid loss
chunks.text:
Signs: pedal goes soft or to the floor, vehicle does not slow down properly, grinding, a brake warning light, fluid near a wheel. Words drivers use: brake nahi lag raha, brake fail, spongy pedal, not stopping.

If brakes fail while moving: shift down through the gears, use the handbrake gradually, and steer away from traffic.

Once stopped, do not drive the vehicle again, not even to the next exit. Brake faults are not something to test or patch at the roadside.

chunks.title: Brake failure or brake fluid loss
chunks.text: This is a tow job. The vehicle should go to a workshop on a tow or flatbed.

chunks.title: Drive chain snapped or slipped (two-wheeler)
chunks.text:
Signs: the engine revs but the bike does not move, a rattle or slap, the chain hanging loose. Words drivers use: chain toot gayi, chain utar gayi, sprocket.

Move the bike off the road on its stand. Keep fingers away from the chain and sprocket if the engine is running.

A mechanic can usually refit a slipped chain or fit a new master link at the roadside. A badly worn chain and sprocket set should be replaced at a workshop soon after.

chunks.title: Clutch failure
chunks.text:
Signs: gears will not engage, engine revs but the vehicle does not move (slipping), a burning smell, a pedal that stays down. Words drivers use: clutch gaya, gear nahi lag raha, clutch slip.

A failed clutch is usually not repairable at the roadside. It often needs the gearbox to be separated in a workshop.

Do not keep forcing gears. Wait in a safe place; the vehicle will normally need towing. A mechanic can confirm whether it is the clutch cable or fluid, which are sometimes simpler fixes.

chunks.title: CNG vehicle breakdown safety
chunks.text:
If you smell gas or hear a hissing sound in a CNG vehicle, switch off the engine, turn off the CNG cylinder valve if you know how, and move everyone away from the vehicle.

Do not smoke or use any flame nearby. Call 112 if you suspect a leak.

Only a trained CNG mechanic should work on the gas system. Many CNG vehicles can switch to petrol, but do not do this if you suspect a leak.

chunks.title: Blown fuse or wiring fault
chunks.text:
Signs: one circuit stops working, such as headlights, indicators, horn or the fuel pump, or a burning plastic smell. Words drivers use: light nahi jal rahi, fuse ud gaya, wiring, short circuit.

If you smell burning plastic or see smoke from wiring, switch off the engine and move everyone away from the vehicle.

A mechanic can find and replace blown fuses and repair simple wiring faults at the roadside. Do not replace a fuse with a higher-rated one or a piece of wire.

chunks.title: Emergency numbers in India
chunks.text:
112 - the national emergency number. Connects you to police, fire and ambulance. Works from any phone.

108 - ambulance service in most states. Call it first if anyone may be injured.

1033 - the national highway helpline, for incidents and assistance on national highways.

When you call, give: your location (highway number, nearest town or kilometre stone), what happened, how many people are with you, and whether anyone is hurt. Stay on the line if asked.

chunks.title: Suspected engine seizure
chunks.text:
Signs: a loud knocking noise, the engine stopping suddenly and refusing to turn, heavy white or blue smoke, the oil warning light. Words drivers use: engine jam, knocking, engine band, oil light.

Do not try to restart. Each attempt can make the damage worse.

This is not a roadside repair. The vehicle needs to be towed to a workshop for inspection. Use the waiting time to arrange safe onward travel for passengers.

chunks.title: Electric vehicle breakdown basics
chunks.text:
If an electric vehicle stops, put it in Park, switch on hazard lights and move people away from traffic.

Do not open or touch high-voltage parts, usually marked with orange cables.

Some electric vehicles should not be towed with the drive wheels on the ground. Tell the mechanic or tow operator that it is an EV so they bring a flatbed.

If you see smoke or smell burning from an EV, move well away and call 112.

chunks.title: Family and child safety on highways
chunks.text:
Children should be the first people moved away from the vehicle and the last to return. Hold small children by the hand and keep them on the side away from traffic.

Never leave children alone in a parked vehicle, especially in heat or with the engine off and windows closed.

Keep water, a torch and something warm handy. Reassure children with a simple plan: we wait here, help is coming.

chunks.title: Family and child safety on highways
chunks.text: If you have small children and the vehicle cannot be fixed quickly, consider safe onward travel or a nearby lodge rather than waiting for hours at the roadside.

chunks.title: Fan belt or serpentine belt snapped
chunks.text:
Signs: a loud squeal or slap, then the battery light and temperature warning come on, power steering may become heavy. Words drivers use: belt toot gaya, fan belt, squealing, screech.

The belt often drives the water pump and alternator. Without it the engine will overheat and the battery will run down.

Switch off and do not restart. A mechanic can usually fit a new belt at the roadside if the pulleys and tensioner are not damaged.

chunks.title: Flat tyre or puncture
chunks.text:
A flat tyre usually shows as the vehicle pulling to one side, a flapping sound, or a wheel sitting low. Common words drivers use: puncture, punchar, pancher, flat, tyre down, hawa nikal gayi.

Pull fully off the carriageway on firm, level ground before doing anything. Switch on hazard lights and get passengers out and behind the barrier.

Do not jack the vehicle on a soft shoulder, sand or a slope. If the ground is not firm, wait for the mechanic rather than trying yourself.

chunks.title: Flat tyre or puncture
chunks.text: A mechanic can usually repair a tubeless puncture with a plug kit, or fit the spare wheel (stepney). Driving any distance on a fully flat tyre can damage the rim and make the repair more expensive.

chunks.title: Water-logged or flooded roads
chunks.text:
Do not drive into water when you cannot see the road surface or how deep it is.

If the engine stops in water, do not try to restart it. Water drawn into the engine can cause serious damage.

If water is rising around the vehicle, leave the vehicle and move to higher ground. Do not stay inside a vehicle in moving water.

A stalled vehicle in water should be towed, not jump-started.

chunks.title: Fuel smell, smoke or fire risk
chunks.text:
If you smell fuel, see smoke from under the bonnet, or see flames: switch off the engine, get everyone out immediately and move well away from the vehicle, upwind if possible.

Call 112. Do not open the bonnet if you suspect a fire; it can feed the fire with air.

Do not return to the vehicle to collect belongings.

Do not smoke or use a lighter near a vehicle that smells of fuel.

chunks.title: Out of fuel
chunks.text:
Signs: the engine sputters and stops, fuel gauge on empty, reserve light was on. Words drivers use: petrol khatam, diesel khatam, fuel over, tank empty, reserve.

Do not keep cranking the starter. It drains the battery and can damage the fuel pump.

A mechanic or fuel stop can bring fuel in an approved can. Diesel vehicles may need the fuel system primed or bled after running dry, which a mechanic can do.

chunks.title: Out of fuel
chunks.text: Never carry fuel inside the passenger cabin, and do not smoke or use open flames near the vehicle while refuelling.

chunks.title: Hazard lights and warning triangle
chunks.text:
Switch on hazard lights the moment you know you have a problem, before you stop.

Place the warning triangle well behind the vehicle in the same lane so approaching drivers have time to react. On a bend or a hill crest, place it before the bend or crest.

Walk to place the triangle facing oncoming traffic, on the side away from the road, and only if it is safe. If it is not safe, skip it and move away from the vehicle.

chunks.title: Hazard lights and warning triangle
chunks.text: If you have no triangle, any reflective or bright object can help, but never risk your safety to place it.

chunks.title: Positioning the vehicle on a highway shoulder
chunks.text:
Stop as far left as the shoulder allows, with the wheels turned away from traffic.

Avoid stopping on bends, bridges, hill crests or just after a toll plaza merge, where other drivers have little time to see you. If the vehicle can still move slowly and safely, continue to a wider spot or a lay-by.

Apply the handbrake and leave the vehicle in gear (or Park).

Everyone should exit on the side away from traffic. Children first.

chunks.title: Jump-start safety
chunks.text:
Only jump-start if you know the correct order and the battery is not cracked, leaking or swollen.

General order: red to the dead battery positive, red to the good battery positive, black to the good battery negative, black to an unpainted metal point on the dead vehicle away from the battery. Remove in reverse order.

Keep sparks and flames away from batteries. Do not lean over the battery while connecting.

If you are unsure, wait for the mechanic. A wrong connection can damage electronics.

chunks.title: Keys locked in or lost key
chunks.text:
Signs: keys visible inside a locked vehicle, a lost key, or a remote or immobiliser that no longer works. Words drivers use: chabi andar reh gayi, key lost, lock ho gaya.

If a child or pet is locked inside, especially in heat, call 112 immediately. Do not wait for a mechanic.

Otherwise, a locksmith-trained mechanic can usually open the vehicle without damage. Keep proof of ownership ready; a responsible mechanic will ask for it.

chunks.title: Safe roadside procedure at night
chunks.text:
1. Signal early and move as far left off the carriageway as possible, ideally past a barrier or onto a wide, firm shoulder.
2. Switch on hazard lights and parking lights straight away.
3. Get every passenger out on the side away from traffic and stand behind the crash barrier or well away from the road.
4. Place a warning triangle, or any reflective object, well behind the vehicle. Only do this if you can walk there safely.

chunks.title: Safe roadside procedure at night
chunks.text:
5. Do not stand between the vehicle and traffic, and do not sit inside a stopped vehicle on a highway shoulder.
6. Share your live location with someone you trust and keep your phone charged.

chunks.title: Engine overheating
chunks.text:
Signs: temperature needle in the red, steam from the bonnet, a sweet smell, warning light. Words drivers use: garam ho gaya, overheat, dhuan, steam, temperature high.

Pull over and switch the engine off. Continuing to drive can seriously damage the engine.

Never open the radiator cap or coolant reservoir while the engine is hot. The system is under pressure and hot coolant can cause serious burns. Wait at least 30 minutes.

chunks.title: Engine overheating
chunks.text: Keep children away from the front of the vehicle. A mechanic will check coolant level, hoses, the fan and the belt before you drive on.

chunks.title: Phone battery and location sharing
chunks.text:
Your phone is your lifeline. Lower screen brightness, close unused apps and turn off mobile data on a second phone to keep it as a reserve.

Share your live location with a family member and send them the RoadSathi guardian link.

If mobile data is weak, an SMS can still get through. RoadSathi accepts an SOS by SMS with your coordinates.

Note a nearby landmark or kilometre stone in case your phone dies.

chunks.title: Plan B: getting people home when the vehicle cannot be fixed
chunks.text:
When the vehicle cannot be repaired tonight, the priority changes from the vehicle to the people.

Options to consider: a verified cab, a bus from a staffed bus station, a train from the nearest station, or a family-safe lodge if children are travelling.

Before leaving the vehicle: remove valuables and documents, take photos of all sides and the odometer, and get a written or digital receipt from whoever takes custody of the vehicle.

chunks.title: Plan B: getting people home when the vehicle cannot be fixed
chunks.text: Share your onward travel details and the cab plate number with a family member.

chunks.title: Radiator or coolant hose leak
chunks.text:
Signs: green, pink or orange liquid dripping under the front, low coolant warning, rising temperature. Words drivers use: paani leak, coolant leak, radiator leak, puddle under car.

Switch off the engine and let it cool. Do not open the radiator cap while hot.

Coolant is harmful if swallowed. Keep children and animals away from the puddle.

A mechanic can often replace a split hose or clamp at the roadside and refill coolant. A cracked radiator usually needs a workshop.

chunks.title: Spark plug or ignition misfire
chunks.text:
Signs: jerking, sputtering, loss of power, the engine shaking at idle, a flashing check-engine light. Words drivers use: jhatke, misfire, engine shaking, pickup nahi.

Drive gently to the nearest safe stopping point. Continuing with a heavy misfire can damage other parts.

A mechanic can check and replace spark plugs or ignition coils at the roadside for most petrol vehicles. Diesel engines do not use spark plugs, so similar symptoms need a different check.

chunks.title: Starter motor failure
chunks.text:
Signs: a single click or whirring sound when you turn the key, but the lights and dashboard work normally. Words drivers use: self start nahi, self not working, engine not turning.

If the lights are bright and only the starter fails, the battery is probably fine.

A mechanic can test the starter and solenoid. Sometimes the starter can be replaced at the roadside. Do not try to push-start an automatic vehicle.

chunks.title: Vehicle stuck in mud or sand
chunks.text:
Do not keep spinning the wheels. It digs the vehicle deeper and can damage the clutch or transmission.

Reduce speed to a gentle crawl, straighten the front wheels, and try moving slowly in a low gear.

Do not stand behind or beside a spinning wheel; debris can be thrown out.

If the vehicle does not move after a few gentle attempts, wait for recovery help.

chunks.title: Suspension, ball joint or axle damage
chunks.text:
Signs: a loud clunk after a pothole, a wheel leaning at an odd angle, steering pulling hard, the vehicle sitting low on one corner. Words drivers use: shocker toota, pothole, wheel tedha, steering kheench raha.

Do not drive a vehicle with a wheel at an odd angle. A failed ball joint can cause the wheel to separate.

This is normally a tow job. A mechanic can assess whether the vehicle is safe to move at very low speed or needs a flatbed.

chunks.title: Tow or repair: how the decision is made
chunks.text:
A roadside repair makes sense when the fault is simple, the parts are available nearby, and the work can be done safely away from traffic. Examples: punctures, flat batteries, a fuse, a slipped chain, running out of fuel.

Towing is the safer choice when the fault affects brakes, steering, suspension or the engine itself, after any collision, or when the work needs the vehicle lifted for a long time.

chunks.title: Tow or repair: how the decision is made
chunks.text: If the mechanic says a repair is not safe at the roadside, accept that advice. A tow costs less than a second breakdown or an accident.

chunks.title: Travelling alone at night
chunks.text:
Share your live location and the details of your breakdown with a trusted person straight away.

If you feel unsafe at the roadside and the vehicle is in a protected place, you may choose to wait inside with doors locked and hazard lights on. On a busy highway shoulder, waiting behind the barrier is usually safer.

Be cautious about accepting help from strangers who stop. Verify any mechanic through the app before opening the vehicle.

If you feel threatened, call 112.

chunks.title: Truck and heavy vehicle breakdown
chunks.text:
Heavy vehicles take up much of the shoulder, so visibility matters even more.

Use hazard lights, parking lights and reflectors. Place warning triangles well behind and, if possible, ahead of the vehicle.

Never work under a raised heavy vehicle without proper stands. Many faults on heavy vehicles need specialist recovery equipment.

The driver and any helpers should wait away from the vehicle, behind the barrier.

chunks.title: Two-wheeler breakdown safety
chunks.text:
Move the bike fully off the road and put it on its stand on firm ground.

Keep your helmet on while near traffic and wear light-coloured or reflective clothing if you have it.

Switch on hazard lights if your bike has them, or keep the tail light on.

Do not push a heavy bike along a busy highway shoulder for long distances. Wait in a safe spot for help.

chunks.title: Tyre burst or sidewall damage
chunks.text:
A burst is a sudden bang followed by loss of control or heavy pulling. Words drivers use: burst, blast, tyre phat gaya, bang, shredded, sidewall cut.

Hold the steering firmly, do not brake hard, and let the vehicle slow down before steering gently to the shoulder.

A burst tyre cannot be patched. It needs the spare wheel or a replacement tyre. Check whether the wheel arch, brake line or body has been damaged before driving again.

chunks.title: Tyre burst or sidewall damage
chunks.text: Do not drive on the rim, even for a short distance. Stay behind the barrier while you wait.

chunks.title: Verifying the mechanic who arrives
chunks.text:
Check that the person who arrives matches the name, photo and vehicle plate shown in the app.

RoadSathi gives you a four-digit arrival code. Read it out only when the mechanic is standing with you; work should not start until they enter it.

Do not hand over keys or documents to someone who cannot confirm the job in the app. If anything feels wrong, step away and call the number shown in the app, or 112.

chunks.title: Breakdown in fog or low visibility
chunks.text:
In fog, a stopped vehicle can be very hard to see until other drivers are close.

Keep hazard lights and parking lights on. Place the warning triangle further back than usual if you can do so safely.

Get everyone out and well away from the road, behind a barrier if there is one. Do not stand behind the vehicle.

Wear or hold something light-coloured or reflective, and use a phone torch to make yourself visible if you have to move near the road.

chunks.title: Breakdown in extreme heat
chunks.text:
In very hot conditions a closed vehicle heats up quickly.

Do not leave anyone, especially children, older people or pets, inside a closed vehicle.

Find shade away from the road, drink water regularly, and cover heads.

Overheating engines are more likely in heat. Do not open the radiator cap on a hot engine.

chunks.title: Breakdown in heavy rain
chunks.text:
In heavy rain other drivers see you late and stopping distances are longer.

Move as far from the carriageway as possible. Keep hazard lights and parking lights on.

Wait behind the barrier rather than inside the vehicle where it is safe to do so, but avoid standing in moving water or under trees and power lines.

Do not attempt repairs on wet, sloping ground. Watch for water rising around the vehicle; if it does, move to higher ground.

chunks.title: When not to attempt a repair yourself
When not to attempt a repair yourself
chunks.text: In these cases keep everyone safe behind the barrier and wait for a trained mechanic.
